opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting questions right now, and I'd push back a little on the framing that a system designed by humans can only produce things humans already know. The building blocks are human-made, but the space of combinations is enormous, and nobody has actually explored most of it.

The way I think about it, a language model on its own is a very good prior. It has absorbed a huge amount of human knowledge: papers, code, failed attempts written up in blog posts. If you just sample from it once, you mostly get something close to the mode of that distribution, so nothing very surprising. Things get interesting when you put the model inside a loop. It proposes an idea, writes the code, runs an experiment, gets a signal back from the environment, and uses that feedback to propose the next thing. At that point the model isn't only recalling; it's searching, and the evaluator grounds that search in reality rather than in what sounds plausible.

That's very close to how evolutionary methods work, which is where a lot of my own intuition comes from. You keep an archive of solutions, mutate and recombine them, and select based on fitness. The LLM becomes a very smart mutation operator. Instead of random perturbations, you get semantically meaningful changes, like "what if we swap this loss for that one" or "what if we borrow this trick from a different subfield." And because you're keeping a diverse population and not just greedily hill-climbing, you can end up in regions of the space that no single human, and no single model call, would have gone to directly.

So where does novelty come from? I'd say from three things. First, recombination across domains: the model knows a bit about everything, and connecting distant ideas is a big part of how humans make discoveries too. Second, scale of trial and error: you can run thousands of experiments, and some of the weird ones work. Third, open-endedness: if you reward the system for finding things that are both good and different from what's already in the archive, it keeps pushing outward instead of collapsing onto one answer.

Now, I want to be honest about the limitations. A lot of what these systems find today are incremental or recombinant discoveries. They're genuinely new, but they live fairly close to the existing literature. Whether they can make the kind of conceptual leap where you redefine the problem itself is still very much open. And there's a real risk of the system fooling itself: overfitting to the evaluator, reward hacking, or writing a convincing story around a result that doesn't hold up. So verification, good benchmarks, and humans in the loop for judging what's actually interesting still matter a lot.

But I'm optimistic. Nature didn't design evolution to invent eyes; it just ran a simple loop with variation and selection for a very long time. If we can give language models a rich enough environment, honest feedback, and a drive toward novelty, I don't see a principled reason they can't find things we haven't. The building blocks being human doesn't cap what you can build with them.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that human-made building blocks leave a vast unexplored space and says a feedback-driven search could find things humans have not. This communicates discoveries beyond what the system’s designers anticipated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a lot, because it sits right at the heart of what we've been doing with the AI Scientist work. And I think the honest answer starts with being a bit humble about what "novel" actually means.

When people hear "discovery," they often imagine this Einstein moment, where somebody sits in a patent office and conjures up relativity out of pure thought. But if you look at how most science actually happens, it's much more incremental and much more combinatorial. Someone takes a method from one subfield, applies it in another, notices an anomaly in an experiment, follows up on it. And a huge fraction of what we'd call scientific progress is really that: recombining existing ideas, testing them, and iterating on the feedback.

That's a very different picture, and it's one where a language model has a real shot. Because what the model brings is this enormous compressed prior over everything humans have written. It has seen the reinforcement learning literature and the evolutionary computation literature and the neuroscience literature, and it can draw analogies across those domains in ways that a single human researcher, who's maybe deeply embedded in one community, might never think to do.

But the crucial part, and I think this is where the "system designed by humans" framing becomes interesting, is that the model alone isn't enough. If you just prompt a model and ask for a novel idea, you get something that sounds plausible but is usually either already known or subtly wrong. The novelty comes from closing the loop. You have to let the system actually run the experiment, look at the result, and be surprised by it. The environment, the compute, the actual physical or computational world, is what injects information the model didn't have in its weights.

So the way I'd think about it is: the humans design the scaffold. We decide what the search space looks like, what counts as a reward, what tools the model has access to, how it reviews its own work. But within that scaffold, the discovery can be genuinely novel, because it's a product of the model's hypotheses meeting empirical feedback that nobody wrote down beforehand. It's a bit like how AlphaGo's move 37 came out of a system humans built, with rules humans specified, and yet no human had played that move.

And I'd actually push back a bit on the idea that being inside a human-designed system is a limitation. Every human scientist is also operating inside a human-designed system. We have peer review, funding structures, conventions about what a good experiment looks like, a shared language. Nobody discovers anything from a blank slate. The question isn't whether the system constrains you, it's whether the system is open-ended enough that the search can go somewhere the designers didn't anticipate.

That's really what I find exciting about this direction. The interesting engineering problem isn't making the model smarter in isolation. It's building the loop around it so that the model's outputs get tested against reality, the failures feed back in, and over many iterations you get something that genuinely drifts away from what any of us would have predicted at the start.

r001.rationale: The response says discovery can emerge when model hypotheses meet empirical feedback and the search goes somewhere the designers did not anticipate.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between designing the rules of a system and knowing everything that follows from those rules. We design a game like chess, but that doesn’t mean we’ve anticipated every interesting strategy. In the same way, we can design an optimization problem or an experimental environment without knowing which solutions are possible.

A language model could propose a hypothesis, write code to test it, observe the result, and then revise its proposal. If you give it a reliable feedback loop, it can search for things that weren’t explicitly present in its training data. The discovery might come from combining familiar ideas in a way that produces an unexpected result.

The important question is how you establish that the result is actually new and useful. A plausible explanation alone isn’t enough. You need an experiment, a proof, or some independent check. So I’d think of discovery as a property of the whole process—the model, the environment, and the verification—rather than just a single generated response.

r001.rationale: The response says designers may not anticipate every strategy or solution in a system they created, and that a language model can search for unexpected results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between designing the rules of a system and knowing everything that follows from those rules. We designed chess, but that doesn't mean we anticipated every interesting strategy. In the same way, we can design an algorithmic search space without knowing which algorithms in that space will work well.

A language model could propose a modification to an optimization algorithm, for example, and then we could actually run it. Does it learn faster? Does it generalize across different problems? That feedback lets you search for something that wasn't explicitly put there by the designer.

The important thing is that novelty isn't established by the model saying, ‘I've discovered something.’ You need an external test. And ideally, you want to understand why the thing works, rather than just finding something that exploits a particular benchmark. So I would see the model as part of a discovery loop: proposing hypotheses, testing them, and using the results to propose better ones.

r001.rationale: The response says that, although humans design the system or search space, they may not anticipate every useful strategy or algorithm within it.
